title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of ON Energy Storage, Inc. in response to comments and protests re Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. proposal to establish Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads under ER26-3650.

documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



    Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                           Docket No. ER26-3650-000


               MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED ANSWER
                         OF ON ENERGY STORAGE, INC.
          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission” or “FERC”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213,

ON Energy Storage, Inc. (“ON.energy”) respectfully moves for leave to answer and submits this

Limited Answer in response to comments and protests concerning the transition and

grandfathering provisions in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”)

proposal to establish Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads (“IRR Proposal”).1


                               MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER


          Rule 213(a)(2) generally prohibits an answer to a protest or an answer unless otherwise

ordered by the decisional authority.2 To the extent leave is required, good cause exists to accept

this Limited Answer. ON.energy filed a timely motion to intervene in this proceeding on

September 18, 2026.3 The September 18, 2026 and September 21, 2026 pleadings present

competing positions on the scope and design of MISO’s transition provisions. Google LLC

(“Google”) supports MISO’s proposed grandfathering framework; the Data Center Coalition

(“DCC”) and Rowan Digital Infrastructure, LLC (“Rowan”) urge greater reliance on objective

ER26-3650-000, Accession No. 20260828-5278 (Aug. 28, 2026) (“MISO Filing”).

  18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).

                                                      1
 evidence of commercial maturity; Entergy Services, LLC (“Entergy”) identifies recently

developed and late-stage projects that may not satisfy MISO’s proposed grandfathering criteria;

and Verrus LLC (“Verrus”) generally supports MISO’s transition approach while seeking clarity

for phased development.4 Other commenters and protestors, including the Organization of MISO

States, Inc. (“OMS”), the Iowa Office of the Consumer Advocate and the other signatories to its

joint protest (“Joint Protestors”), and Sierra Club and the other Public Interest Organizations

(“PIOs”), question whether development status should determine exemption from the ramp and

ride-through requirements, whether proposed Section 37A.II.3 permits MISO to act before an

exempt Large Load causes a reliability problem, and how MISO will address the combined effect

of multiple exempt Large Loads.5


        This Limited Answer responds to the positions already placed before the Commission by

explaining why legitimate reliance interests can be protected through objective and time-limited

transition treatment without foreclosing prospective assessment of the reliability consequences of

ride-through exemptions. In particular, ON.energy asks the Commission to condition acceptance

of MISO’s transition provisions on an outside energization date for Large Loads that receive

transition treatment based on the MTEP/EPR Condition or any broader commercial-maturity test,

and to direct MISO to clarify that exempt Large Loads will be subject to prospective, system-level

reliability review under proposed Section 37A.II.3. ON.energy does not seek to introduce new

(“DCC Comments”); Limited Protest of Entergy Services, LLC, Docket No. ER26-3650-000, at 3 (Sept. 18, 2026)
(“Entergy Protest”); Comments of Rowan Digital Infrastructure, LLC, Docket No. ER26-3650-000, at 2-3 (filed Sept.

Requirements for Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3650-000, at 4 (Sept. 18, 2026) (“Verrus Comments”).
5
  See Notice of Intervention and Comments of the Organization of MISO States, Inc., Docket No. ER26-3650-000, at
4-5 (Sept. 18, 2026) (“OMS Comments”); Joint Protest of the Iowa Office of the Consumer Advocate et al., Docket
No. ER26-3650-000, at 3-4 (Sept. 18, 2026) (“Joint Protest”); Protest of Sierra Club et al., Docket No. ER26-3650-
000, at 2-3, 12-15 (Sept. 18, 2026) (“PIO Protest”).


                                                        2
 technical ride-through, modeling, or equipment requirements, and it does not address the other

issues raised in the comments and protests, such as the rule of reason, the definition of Large Load,

forecasting, or cost allocation. ON.energy submits this Limited Answer promptly after the

pleadings it addresses and well before the requested December 4, 2026 effective date. Acceptance

of this Limited Answer will assist the Commission in resolving an issue already squarely presented

by the parties and will not delay the proceeding or prejudice any participant. The Commission has

accepted otherwise-prohibited answers where they provide information that assists its decision-

making.6


        Accordingly, ON.energy respectfully requests that the Commission grant leave to answer

and consider the Limited Answer below.


                                                LIMITED ANSWER


I.      ON.energy Supports Reasonable, Objective, and Time-Limited Transition Treatment
        that Protects Legitimate Reliance Interests.

        MISO’s filing establishes three principal transition categories. First, Large Loads with a

Service Commencement Date on or before December 4, 2026 are fully exempt from proposed

Section 37A with respect to the portion of the Large Load that has procured Transmission Service

as of the Service Commencement Date. Second, projects that meet the MTEP/EPR Condition are

subject to the visibility requirements but are exempt from the ramp and ride-through requirements.

Third, certain projects submitted to EPR between June 19 and October 31, 2026 may receive a

ride-through waiver only if MISO determines that the exemption would not have an adverse




6
  See, e.g., Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 187 FERC ¶ 61,202, at P 24 (2024); Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194
FERC ¶ 61,031, at P 58 (2026) (accepting answers because they provided information that assisted the Commission
in its decision-making process).


                                                        3
 reliability impact and compliance would impose significant costs.7 ON.energy does not challenge

the first category, which applies to Large Loads taking service by the proposed effective date, or

the third, which conditions relief on a determination that the exemption would not have an adverse

reliability impact. ON.energy does not advocate automatic retroactive application of new ride-

through requirements to facilities already operating under existing requirements. Its concern is

with the second category, which exempts qualifying Large Loads from the ride-through and ramp

requirements without any limit on when they must begin taking service. As explained below,

ON.energy asks that the second category, and any broader eligibility test the Commission may

adopt, be bounded by an outside energization date.


        ON.energy agrees with these commenters that transition provisions should recognize

legitimate reliance interests, although it does not endorse each eligibility test they propose. For

example, Google emphasizes commercial certainty and investments made under the rules in effect

when projects were developed.8 DCC argues that MTEP or EPR status is not a reliable proxy for

the commercial maturity of a Large Load project and proposes that grandfathering instead turn on

objective evidence of material commercial arrangements, such as executed interconnection,

transmission service, or utility service agreements, or major equipment orders, with qualifying

projects exempt from the ride-through and ramp requirements.9 Rowan similarly asks that

transition relief account for objective evidence of project maturity, procurement, engineering, and

construction.10 Verrus generally supports MISO’s transition provisions and emphasizes the phased

buildout of large load campuses.11 Entergy likewise notes that certain recently developed projects


7
  MISO Filing, Transmittal Letter at 13-14; id., Proposed Tariff § 37A.II; id., Tab C, Prepared Direct Testimony of
Beibei Li at 18-22 (“Li Testimony”).
8
  Google Comments at 1, 3-4.
9
  DCC Comments at 26-29.
10
   Rowan Comments at 2-3.
11
   Verrus Comments at 4.


                                                        4
 and projects in the late stages of negotiations may not satisfy MISO’s proposed grandfathering

criteria or may qualify only for limited exemptions.12


        Taken together, these comments identify a legitimate need to account for genuine late-stage

reliance. ON.energy agrees that this need should be accommodated but believes the relief should

be objectively bounded in time, under whichever eligibility test the Commission accepts, including

any test based on commercial maturity, as DCC and Rowan request. This need can be met without

open-ended relief for projects that are still being designed and developed.


        An outside energization date would meet that need, and MISO’s second category does not

currently include one. MISO explains that tying transition treatment to MTEP and EPR status

recognizes the “more immediate, non-speculative, nature of the Load additions,” and it describes

the October 31, 2026 cutoff for the third category as establishing “a finite transition period, after

which prospective projects are expected to account for MISO’s ride-through requirements as part

of their development and design.”13 The second category, by contrast, has a fixed eligibility date

but no limit on when a qualifying Large Load must begin taking service. DCC itself observes that,

under the MTEP/EPR Condition, a Large Load customer that “may have to wait several years to

commence operations” could nonetheless qualify for exemption based on the timing of its

associated transmission submissions.14 The PIOs similarly read the Commission’s directive to

propose a “reasonable implementation period” as implying “a period after which implementation

will be completed.”15 An outside energization date would align the second category with MISO’s




12
   Entergy Protest at 3.
13
   MISO Filing, Transmittal Letter at 14; Li Testimony at 19:20-23, 22:1-4.
14
   DCC Comments at 27.
15
   PIO Protest at 14.


                                                         5
 own rationale without disturbing the reliance interests of projects that are genuinely near

completion.


         The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”) is addressing the same problem

MISO faces here: establishing clear and achievable ride-through requirements that maintain

system stability without being unduly burdensome to Large Loads. ERCOT’s framework shows

that those objectives can be pursued together, and it offers a useful model for MISO. In particular,

ERCOT’s transition framework shows that an outside energization date can work alongside the

kind of commercial-milestone evidence DCC and Rowan propose. ERCOT’s ride-through

exemption turns on objective milestones achieved by its November 14, 2025 grandfathering date,

such as operation or written approval to energize, or executed interconnection agreements together

with notice to proceed and funding of the required interconnection facilities. For a Large

Computational Load that was not required to be in ERCOT’s interim Large Load interconnection

process, the exemption also requires a written attestation from the interconnecting utility and Initial

Energization by December 31, 2026.16 ERCOT thus tied eligibility to milestones achieved before

its grandfathering date and, for one category of projects, to a defined outside energization date.

That category offers the closest parallel to MISO’s situation. ERCOT applied its outside date to

loads that were not required to go through its interim Large Load interconnection process, and

MISO does not currently have a Load interconnection process at all; it relies instead on MTEP and

EPR status.17 A similarly defined outside boundary in MISO could complement, rather than

displace, the objective evidence of commercial maturity urged by DCC and Rowan, and could

address the circumstances Entergy describes for recently developed and late-stage projects. It


16
   See ERCOT, Nodal Operating Guides § 2.15(1)(a)-(d) (eff. Aug. 1, 2026); see also id. § 2.6.4(1) (parallel exemption
from frequency ride-through requirements).
17
   Li Testimony at 19:17-20.


                                                          6
  would also advance the commercial certainty emphasized by Google by allowing developers to

 know in advance the period during which transition treatment is available.


         ON.energy therefore requests that the Commission condition acceptance of the second

 transition category on an outside energization date, so that transition treatment under that category

 is available only to Large Loads whose Service Commencement Date, the measure MISO already

 uses for the first category, occurs within approximately one year after the effective date of the new

 requirements. ON.energy recommends approximately one year as a reasonable outer limit and

 would leave the precise date and implementing details to MISO on compliance. If the Commission

 also accepts DCC’s and Rowan’s requests to base eligibility on commercial commitments, the

 same outside date should apply to that broader eligibility. A boundary of that general magnitude

 would separate projects with genuine near-term implementation constraints from projects that

 remain sufficiently prospective to account for ride-through requirements before energization,

 consistent with the Show Cause Order’s direction that MISO “propose a reasonable

 implementation period to ensure minimal disruption to such existing commercial arrangements”

 and “allow a reasonable amount of time to finalize ongoing agreements that are nearing

 completion.”18


II.      Commercial Reliance Does Not, by Itself, Resolve the Reliability Questions Presented
         by a Ride-Through Exemption.

         DCC would exempt qualifying projects from the ride-through and ramp requirements based

 on objective evidence of commercial commitments, and Rowan would extend transition relief on

 a similar basis.19 OMS and the Joint Protestors, by contrast, observe that the reliability risks of



 18
    Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 5 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”); see MISO Filing,
 Transmittal Letter at 13; Google Comments at 4.
 19
    DCC Comments at 28-29; Rowan Comments at 3.


                                                         7
 Large Loads do not necessarily depend on when a load becomes operational.20 Both concerns are

legitimate. The existence of legitimate commercial reliance addresses a different question from

whether exempting a Computational Load from disturbance ride-through requirements can be

accommodated without creating a material reliability concern. A project may have substantial sunk

investment and genuine reliance interests while still presenting disturbance behavior that requires

study or mitigation. Conversely, a late-stage project may present no material reliability concern

and therefore warrant transition treatment without additional measures. ON.energy believes both

commercial reliance and reliability should be considered, but agrees with Google that “ensuring

electric reliability must remain job number one.” Where a material reliability concern is identified,

grid reliability should control.21


         MISO’s own proposal recognizes this distinction for one category of in-flight projects. For

projects submitted to EPR between June 19 and October 31, 2026, MISO does not grant an

automatic ride-through exemption. Instead, MISO may waive the ride-through requirement only

where the applicable reliability assessment demonstrates that operation without full ride-through

capability would not have an adverse reliability impact and compliance would result in significant

costs. MISO’s supporting testimony states that, where such a reliability determination cannot be

made, appropriate ride-through capability or mitigation would still be required.22


         That same distinction should govern any request to broaden transition eligibility for other

in-flight projects. Objective commercial commitments may be relevant to whether a project

   OMS Comments at 5 (“reliability risks associated with Large Loads do not necessarily depend on when a load
becomes operational”); Joint Protest at 3 (“Large Loads have reliability impacts regardless of operational date”).
21
   Google Comments at 5; see also id. at 1; Show Cause Order at P 58 (integrating large loads “poses specific
challenges to transmission system operation given their size, operational behavior, and unique potential to impact the
transmission system”); OMS Comments at 5 (asking “whether loads that present material reliability risks should be
subject to appropriate reliability requirements regardless of their development status”).
22
   MISO Filing, Proposed Tariff § 37A.II.2(b)(ii); Li Testimony at 21:6-22:13.


                                                          8
   qualifies for transition consideration, but they should not substitute for evaluating the reliability

  consequences of the resulting ride-through exemption. Rowan’s own formulation reflects this

  distinction: it would provide relief where compliance would require material redesign or

  replacement of previously procured equipment “without a demonstrated reliability necessity.”23

  ON.energy agrees with that formulation. If the Commission broadens transition eligibility based

  on commercial commitments, as DCC and Rowan request, ON.energy asks that any resulting

  exemption remain subject to MISO’s authority to require ride-through capability or other

  mitigation where MISO identifies a material reliability concern, as discussed in Section III below.


III.      Prospective Reliability Review Can Provide Greater Commercial Certainty While
          Preserving MISO’s Proposed Backstop.

          Google describes the “notwithstanding” language in proposed Section 37A.II.3 as

  important because it “allows [MISO] to continue monitoring the operational risks introduced by

  certain large loads and modify its approach where necessary to address reliability risks.”24

  ON.energy agrees that this authority is an important backstop and should be preserved, and

  believes it will work best, for both reliability and commercial certainty, if MISO can apply it

  prospectively. A study before energization can identify a material reliability concern while the

  customer still has time to address it with less disruption, rather than after a problem has occurred

  in operation. DCC itself recognizes that “the timing of any such evaluation and the compliance

  timeline afforded to an affected customer will determine whether revocation is a manageable

  transition or a significant disruption to the customer’s operations.”25




  23
     Rowan Comments at 3.
  24
     Google Comments at 5.
  25
     DCC Comments at 13.


                                                    9
         MISO’s tariff language does not expressly establish a prospective screening requirement

for automatically exempt facilities. The proposed tariff states that MISO may require compliance

where operation of a Large Load “results in a material adverse effect” and leaves the process for

making that determination, as well as the requirements to be imposed, to the Business Practices

Manual.26 The PIOs read that language as ambiguous regarding whether MISO may impose

requirements before an exempt Large Load has caused a reliability problem.27 DCC has separately

raised concerns that the standards and procedures governing withdrawal of an exemption are not

sufficiently defined in the tariff.28 ON.energy agrees in part with both concerns. Section 37A.II.3

should permit MISO to act before an exempt Large Load causes a reliability problem, as the PIOs

urge, and the criteria and process MISO will apply should be objective and known in advance, as

DCC urges. ON.energy takes no position here on whether those details belong in the tariff or the

Business Practices Manual.


        ON.energy believes that a prospective, study-based process can respond to both the PIOs’

and DCC’s concerns. For a facility that has not yet energized, MISO can evaluate expected

disturbance performance before operation and inform the affected customer of any identified

reliability limitation while the customer still has an opportunity to implement ride-through

capability or another technically appropriate mitigation. For an operating or substantially

completed facility, MISO can account for legitimate reliance interests when determining the timing

and scope of any necessary action. In either case, ON.energy believes the relevant measure is the

facility’s performance at its Point(s) of Withdrawal, and it defers to MISO’s Business Practices

Manual process on the study methods and criteria used to evaluate that performance. ON.energy


26
   MISO Filing, Proposed Tariff § 37A.II.3.
27
   PIO Protest at 12.
28
   DCC Comments at 12-13, 15-16.


                                                10
  does not ask the Commission or MISO to prescribe any particular equipment, architecture, or

 technology.


           This approach can provide developers with more certainty, not less. DCC seeks assurance

 that exemptions, once granted, will not be “summarily revoked based on a subjective MISO

 assessment without regard to the stage of development of their facilities.”29 Rather than granting

 an exemption subject to an undefined possibility that MISO may later impose additional

 requirements after an operating problem emerges, a prospective assessment can identify before

 energization the circumstances in which mitigation may be required. Nothing in this approach

 requires eliminating MISO’s Section 37A.II.3 backstop or subjecting all grandfathered loads to

 the full requirements irrespective of demonstrated need. ON.energy therefore requests that the

 Commission accept Section 37A.II.3 and confirm, or direct MISO to clarify on compliance, that

 MISO will evaluate exempt Large Loads before energization, using objective criteria established

 in advance, and will require ride-through capability or other appropriate mitigation where that

 evaluation identifies a material reliability concern.


IV.        System-Level Review Should Consider the Aggregate Amount and Electrical
           Concentration of Exempt Computational Load.

           The PIOs note that the IRR Proposal does not explain how MISO would address

 circumstances in which Large Loads that would not individually cause a material adverse effect

 on reliability could do so in combination.30 ON.energy agrees the question warrants attention and

 believes MISO should address it by evaluating exempt Computational Load, including load that

 has not yet energized, in its system stability studies and by requiring an appropriate reliability




 29
      DCC Comments at 15-16.
 30
      PIO Protest at 13.


                                                  11
 response where those studies identify a material reliability concern. Ride-through risk is not solely

an individual-project question. The reliability consequence of an exemption can depend on the

aggregate amount, location, electrical concentration, and modeled coincident response of similarly

situated Computational Loads.31 A facility that may not present a material concern when evaluated

alone may contribute to a different system response when considered with other exempt load

exposed to the same disturbance. This kind of coincident response has already been observed in

ERCOT and in the Eastern Interconnection, where MISO also operates, and ERCOT has accounted

for it in its ride-through framework, as discussed below.32


        Several parties have raised concerns regarding the amount of existing and in-flight Large

Load that could receive full or partial transition treatment.33 ON.energy does not contend that the

aggregate quantity cited in those pleadings would disconnect simultaneously or that a nameplate

total, standing alone, establishes a reliability violation. The analysis should focus on the amount

and electrical concentration of exempt Computational Load that could respond coincidentally to a

credible voltage or frequency disturbance.


        ERCOT’s experience is relevant to MISO because the underlying mechanism does not

depend on market design: in any system, the question is whether the combined response of exempt

load exposed to a common disturbance stays within that system’s stability limits. ERCOT has

recognized that multiple large electronic load facilities “at nearby locations could trip or transfer

potentially across multiple facilities”).
32
   See NERC, Incident Review: Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions at 2, 8 (Jan. 8, 2025)
(approximately 1,500 MW of data center load reduction coincident with a July 10, 2024 transmission disturbance in

(ERCOT identified 26 ride-through events involving indirect load loss greater than 100 MW from one or more crypto
facilities between January 2023 and September 2025); PIO Protest at 4-5 (describing a July 2026 event in PJM in
which approximately 3.8 GW of load tripped offline).
33
   See OMS Comments at 5; Joint Protest at 3; PIO Protest at 2-3.


                                                       12
 load at a level exceeding frequency and voltage stability limits during a common system

disturbance.”34 When asked to move its grandfathering date, ERCOT evaluated the additional

amount of exempt Large Load and concluded that expanding the exempt population could worsen

existing reliability risk and increase the likelihood of real-time curtailment “to maintain necessary

System Operating Limits to prevent load loss exceeding frequency stability thresholds.”35 ERCOT

also evaluates Large Loads prospectively: new Large Loads must be included in its quarterly

stability assessment to qualify for Initial Energization, and under its interim ride-through

assessment it provided that energization would be conditioned on an appropriate System Operating

Limit or Interconnection Reliability Operating Limit where the assessment identified a stability

concern.36 ERCOT has since reported that its studies identified a load loss limit of 3,200 MW “to

ensure frequency stability and reliable grid operations,” and that its most recent quarterly stability

assessment identified three groups of Large Loads where a disturbance could cause a loss above

that limit from loads without ride-through capability operating at or near full consumption. In each

group, combined approved capacity already exceeds the limit, but ERCOT reports maximum

simultaneous consumption well below it. ERCOT will implement constraints as actual

consumption approaches the limit.37 Importantly, the aggregate reliability effect of transition

treatment can be evaluated prospectively through system studies. MISO’s limits and load

concentrations will differ from ERCOT’s, and ON.energy does not ask MISO to adopt ERCOT’s

3,200 MW limit or other ERCOT-specific thresholds.

   ERCOT Comments on Nodal Operating Guide Revision Request 282, 282NOGRR-17, at 2 (Mar. 27, 2026).
35

36

Requesting Initial Energization Before July 1, 2026 (Jan. 31, 2026).
37
   ERCOT Board Update, slide 6.


                                                       13
        ON.energy therefore requests that the Commission direct MISO to clarify on compliance

that MISO will evaluate the aggregate amount and location of exempt Computational Load,

including load that has not yet energized, through appropriate post-fault voltage and frequency

studies and other dynamic analysis, and, where those studies identify a material reliability concern,

will require an appropriate reliability response, such as an operating limit or other mitigation, under

criteria established in advance. Where the studies demonstrate that an exemption can be

accommodated without material adverse effect, the project’s reliance interests can be respected

without unnecessary additional requirements. Setting limits proactively and updating them as new

Computational Load approaches energization, as ERCOT does, would help protect grid stability

and give developers of facilities without ride-through capability earlier notice of any limits that

may apply.


V.     Conclusion

       For the foregoing reasons, ON.energy respectfully requests that the Commission grant

leave to answer and accept this Limited Answer. In acting on MISO’s filing and the competing

requests concerning transition treatment, ON.energy requests that the Commission: (1) condition

acceptance of the second transition category on an outside energization date limiting transition

treatment to Large Loads whose Service Commencement Date occurs within approximately one

year after the effective date, with the precise date specified by MISO on compliance; (2) if it

broadens transition eligibility based on commercial commitments, as DCC and Rowan request,

apply the same outside date to that broader eligibility and keep any resulting exemption subject to

Section 37A.II.3; and (3) direct MISO to clarify on compliance that, under Section 37A.II.3,

MISO will evaluate exempt Large Loads, individually and in the aggregate, before energization

using objective criteria established in advance, and will require ride-through capability or other



                                                  14
 appropriate mitigation where that evaluation identifies a material reliability concern. These

requests would preserve reasonable protection for legitimate reliance interests while keeping

transition eligibility objective and time-limited and preserving prospective, system-level

assessment of material reliability risks.
